findings.evidence: The benefits team tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year... the people operations office updates the equipment catalog each quarter. ... The finance liaison reviews the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year. ... The people operations office tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year.
findings.fix: Name one office as the owner of this task and state it once; if more than one office is genuinely involved, say explicitly how their roles differ instead of repeating the same sentence under a different actor each time.
findings.location: Program Overview, paragraph 1 and 2; Special Cases; Questions and Updates
findings.violation: The near-identical sentence about tracking the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year is attributed to three different named offices (the benefits team, the finance liaison, the people operations office) in three separate sections, with no statement of whether these are the same office under different names or three distinct offices sharing the duty, so the reader cannot tell who actually owns this task.

findings.evidence: The workspace must sit inside the employee's primary residence... A workspace located in a shared coworking space does not qualify... A workspace used only occasionally for calls does not meet the bar... The reviewer confirms the workspace address matches... A workspace shared with a roommate can still qualify... The stipend covers only the equipment placed inside that confirmed workspace, nothing located elsewhere in the home.
findings.fix: Open the paragraph with the governing rule ('the stipend covers only equipment inside a confirmed home workspace') and follow it with the conditions and exceptions that qualify it.
findings.violation: The paragraph opens with five sentences of conditions, disqualifications, and exceptions about what counts as a qualifying workspace before the sixth sentence finally states the governing rule: what the stipend actually covers. A reader has to hold five unresolved conditions in mind before the rule they modify ever appears.

findings.evidence: Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt.
findings.fix: Move this content beside or into the How to Apply section, at the point where the reader actually begins the process, or delete it if it duplicates that section.
findings.location: Request Steps section (appears after How to Apply, Approval Timeline, Required Documentation, Reimbursement Amounts, Restrictions and Exceptions, and Terminology Notes)
findings.violation: This section restates the start of the application process, but it appears after six other sections that already walked the reader through applying, being approved, and being reimbursed. A reader who reaches it this late in the document, having already read the full application procedure, has no way to tell whether this is a new, different process or a stray restatement of one already covered, because the document's order does not track the reader's actual task sequence.

findings.evidence: 71-word sentence, 5 subordinate-clause markers: Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 71 words with 5 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: The determination of stipend eligibility happens before any payment goes out. The escalation of repeat requests happens automatically within the same quarter.
findings.fix: Name the actual role or office that determines eligibility and the one that escalates repeat requests, and make each the sentence's subject: 'The benefits team determines eligibility before...' / 'Finance escalates repeat requests...'
findings.violation: Both sentences in this section route their action through an abstraction (the determination, the escalation) rather than naming who determines eligibility or who escalates repeat requests, even though the section is specifically about assigning responsibility. A reader cannot learn who is actually responsible for either action from the one section whose job is to say.

findings.evidence: Special Cases: The finance liaison reviews the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year. Staff can request a printed copy from the benefits team at any time. / Questions and Updates: The people operations office tracks the stipend budget at the start of the fiscal year. Every entry carries a date stamp so the record stays easy to audit.
findings.fix: Either fold this repeated administrative note into Program Overview once, or replace these two sections with content that actually matches their own headings.
findings.location: Special Cases and Questions and Updates sections
findings.violation: A reader who reads only the first and last sentence of 'Special Cases' or of 'Questions and Updates' cannot connect what is there to what the heading promises: neither section discusses a special case or a question or an update, each instead repeats the budget-tracking sentence from Program Overview nearly verbatim under a different named office. Across the document these two sections, plus Program Overview, add no new theme, so the reader cannot resolve what either heading is actually about.

findings.evidence: 71-word sentence: Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee whenever the benefits team confirms that the role genuinely requires a second device because fieldwork regularly takes the employee away from the single fixed desk that the standard equipment list assumes every applicant has for the whole benefit year while the finance office tracks the second device against the same annual amount that the equipment catalog publishes for each category.
findings.fix: Move subordinate clauses and modifiers after the main clause, not between its subject and verb.
findings.violation: At 71 words, with 0 comma-set-off clause(s) and 5 subordinate-clause marker(s), the sentence stacks interruptions between its subject and its main verb instead of holding the main clause together.

findings.evidence: The benefits team coordinates every stipend request from intake to payout. The team logs each request the moment it arrives. ... The determination of stipend eligibility happens before any payment goes out. The escalation of repeat requests happens automatically within the same quarter.
findings.fix: Either state who each section is for (e.g. a note that these two sections describe internal processing only) or cut them, since they add no actionable information for the employee applying for the stipend.
findings.location: Program Coordination and Review Responsibility sections
findings.violation: The document never establishes a single clear intended reader. Most sections instruct the employee-applicant directly on what to submit and when, but Program Coordination and Review Responsibility narrate internal team hand-offs that give the applicant no action and read as if written for internal staff, with no signal marking them as background rather than instructions to follow.

findings.evidence: Full-time employees ... are eligible for the home-office equipment stipend. ... In addition, eligibility for the workspace stipend depends on several details the reviewer checks one at a time.
findings.fix: Use one name for the benefit throughout, or state explicitly that 'workspace stipend' refers to the same home-office equipment stipend's location requirement.
findings.violation: The Eligibility section names the benefit 'the home-office equipment stipend' in its first paragraph and then 'the workspace stipend' in its third paragraph, with no statement that the two terms name the same benefit, leaving the reader to infer from proximity alone whether a second, separately-named stipend with its own eligibility rules is being introduced.

findings.evidence: Employees must submit the receipt, the manager's approval form, and the original purchase order before the review begins.
findings.fix: Reformat the inline items as a numbered or bulleted list.
findings.violation: The sentence embeds three or more comma- or semicolon-separated parallel items inline rather than presenting them as a formatted list.

findings.evidence: Additionally, employees shall retain receipts for one year after the purchase date.
findings.violation: The sentence states a binding requirement using shall or an indirect requirement phrasing instead of must.

findings.evidence: The finance office conducts an evaluation of every submitted receipt before it approves the amount.
findings.fix: Restate the nominalized noun as the sentence's main verb.
findings.violation: The action is buried inside the noun 'evaluation', carried by a generic support verb, instead of stated as the sentence's own main verb.
